paper.title: Long-term impact of ChatGPT-4 on music students' creative and analytical skills: A follow-up study
paper.pdf_filename: Zhou et al (2026) - Long-term impact of ChatGPT-4 on music students' creative and analytical skills.pdf
paper.version_read: Published journal version: Thinking Skills and Creativity 63 (2027) 102344; DOI 10.1016/j.tsc.2026.102344. Received 8 October 2025; revised 25 July 2026; accepted 22 August 2026; available online 23 August 2026 (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: Among 74 music students analyzed in a study reporting class-level random assignment, the ChatGPT-4 group had higher adjusted expert-rated creativity than the traditional-instruction group (4.71 vs 4.35; F(1, 69) = 7.216, p = .009, η² = .096; p. 12, Tables 5-6) and a steeper reported creativity growth slope (0.315 vs 0.210; p. 9, Table 3).
paper.shared_samples: Zhou, W., & Kim, Y. (2024). Innovative music education: An empirical assessment of ChatGPT-4's impact on student learning experiences. Education and Information Technologies, 29, 20855-20881. Same cohort. The introduction describes that study as having '74 undergraduate music students in Korea' (p. 2). The present paper collects new data in a new 24-week intervention and does not reanalyze the earlier data. In the earlier study only the AI-condition students received structured ChatGPT-supported learning, so prior ChatGPT use is a covariate here. Whether students kept their earlier condition is not stated.

studies.label: 24-week classroom intervention: ChatGPT-4-supported vs traditional music instruction
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Random assignment was at the class level (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). Neither the MANCOVA nor the latent growth model reports class-clustered standard errors or class-level random effects (PDF pp. 8-9, Sections 3.7 and 4; PDF p. 12, Tables 5-6). The growth factors describe students. Class counts and the allocation procedure are unreported; participant-level precision does not account for the randomized classes.

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT-4 supported)
arms.description: Students used ChatGPT-4 throughout music coursework for melodic, harmonic, and structural suggestions, compositional feedback, improvisation prompts, analytical checks, and arranging support. They were encouraged to evaluate, adapt, and integrate its output and submitted screenshots or links of their interactions. Same instructor as control (PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 3.2 and 3.6 and Table 1).

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Equivalent music tasks with traditional teacher-led instruction, textbooks, class notes, lectures, handouts, and teacher feedback, without AI augmentation. Same instructor as the experimental group (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2 and Table 1).

studies.task: Second-year Bachelor of Music students produced compositions, recorded improvisations, reharmonizations, stylistic adaptations, and arrangements, with accompanying analytical tasks, during normal coursework.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-4 (identified as ChatGPT-4o in Section 3.1)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.1: "the newer generation of ChatGPT-4 (i.e., ChatGPT-4o)"; PDF p. 4, Section 2.3, system announcement cited as OpenAI (2024); PDF p. 18, References: "OpenAI. (2024). GPT-4o system card."

preregistration.where: No preregistration or trial registration is stated in the complete article; PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, reports ethics approval only.

studies.shared_sample: Drawn from the cohort in Zhou and Kim (2024), Innovative music education: An empirical assessment of ChatGPT-4’s impact on student learning experiences, Education and Information Technologies, DOI 10.1007/s10639-024-12705-z. This article reports new follow-up coursework data, not a reanalysis of the earlier outcomes. Earlier AI-condition students had structured ChatGPT exposure; whether current allocation retained earlier conditions is not stated. PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; PDF p. 19, References.

estimates.outcome: Adjusted expert-rated creativity of musical products
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Two external assessors with expertise in music theory, composition, and creativity research independently scored students' creative products, blinded to identity, condition, and submission timing. The rubric has four dimensions, each on a seven-point scale: originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, and expressive impact. It draws on Webster's model and the Consensual Assessment Technique. The paper does not specify dimension/rater aggregation or report inter-rater reliability for the output scores (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3; PDF p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5).

paper_effect.standardizer: The table labels the effect size η². It does not say partial eta squared or give a formula/standardizer.

sources.quote: A quasi-experimental design was employed with 74 undergraduate music students assigned to an experimental group (n= 36) and a control group (n= 38).

estimates.notes: The means are adjusted marginal means, and the F test is the Group / Creativity univariate test following MANCOVA. The covariates are prior ChatGPT use, Week 1 creativity, and Week 1 analytical skills (PDF p. 9, Results RQ2). The paper calls Week 1 scores baseline and describes baseline tasks as preceding intervention (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1), so this is retained as the reported baseline-adjusted contrast. The exact timing of Week 1 measurement relative to initial AI access remains unresolved because Table 1 places supported coursework in the opening weeks. The MANCOVA dependent variable's measurement occasion or aggregation is unspecified; this is not identified as a final-session score. The analysis is at the student level: Table 6 supplies analyzed student counts, not counts of ratings or submissions. The total is the main-study count printed in the abstract, whose arm counts match Table 6; it was not inferred from degrees of freedom. AI was available while the intervention products were made. Immediate identifies assessment during supported coursework; no outcome after AI withdrawal is reported. Students remained in separate instructional groups, so repeated assessments do not make this a within-person AI crossover. se_basis=participant describes the reported student-level analysis and does not establish valid precision for class randomization. No class-adjusted uncertainty, arm SD, mean difference, difference SE, or confidence interval is printed. No missing statistic was computed.

estimates.outcome: Mean latent linear growth slope of expert-rated musical creativity
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Two external assessors with expertise in music theory, composition, and creativity research independently scored students' creative products, blinded to identity, condition, and submission timing. The rubric has four dimensions, each on a seven-point scale: originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, and expressive impact. It draws on Webster's model and the Consensual Assessment Technique. The paper does not specify dimension/rater aggregation or report inter-rater reliability for the output scores (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3; PDF p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). The linear latent growth model uses repeated student assessments; arm mean fields contain estimated means of the latent slope factors (PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1 and Table 3).

sources.locator: PDF p. 9, Table 3, Creativity / Slope row (Experimental and Control: Est., Std. Err., p-value)

estimates.notes: The mean and SE fields contain arm-specific latent mean slopes and their standard errors, not final creativity-score levels or a treatment-indicator regression coefficient. Results RQ1 explicitly compares growth across groups (PDF p. 8), so the reported arm parameters are retained as the descriptive slope comparison. No between-arm slope difference, difference SE, confidence interval, or test is printed. Table 3 prints < .000 for each arm parameter; those within-arm tests against zero are preserved in the source quote and are not a contrast p-value. Three-decimal table precision is preserved in that quote, including 0.210 and 0.010; rounded restatements in the prose are not additional estimates. No growth-model-specific analyzed participant count is printed, so n_treatment, n_control, and n_total are null. The latent growth factors describe individual students over repeated submissions, making participant the analysis unit and the reported uncertainty basis; no class effects or class-adjusted uncertainty are reported. Repeated measurement within each instructional group is not randomized crossover: within_person is null. AI remained available during the intervention, so this is with_ai, not after_ai. The time-step unit is unresolved: the procedure describes biweekly submissions across two semesters, while the figure labels occasions as weeks. No time conversion was made. Figure 1 has no numeric labels on the plotted points, and no occasion-specific means were read from the graph. Initial intercepts and random-factor variances were not treated as intervention effects or observed-score SDs.
estimates.primary_override_reason: Rule 2: Neither candidate is explicitly designated primary, but the abstract reports the group difference in growth trajectories, corresponding to the latent creativity slope. The adjusted comparison is introduced as a subsequent check of whether the advantage remains after covariate adjustment, so the growth specification reported in the abstract takes priority under rule 2. (PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1 and Table 3; PDF p. 9, Results RQ2 (adjusted follow-up).: "Results indicated that the experimental group began with higher initial levels and demonstrated steeper growth trajectories, reflecting a Matthew effect, while the control group displayed compensatory tendencies.")

not_extracted.what: Pilot study used to calibrate creativity and analytical-thinking rubrics
not_extracted.reason: The pilot used twelve students outside the main sample, with no randomized AI comparison or numerical treatment effect reported; it is also below the minimum participant count. PDF p. 7, Section 3.4; PDF p. 5, Section 3.1.

Exclude the A-only estimate. The paper scores an accompanying analytical task separately from the creative musical product (PDF p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.6). Its rubric measures harmonic/structural labeling accuracy, theoretical justification, reasoning depth, and transfer; it is a music-analysis competence outcome, not creativity, diversity, or usefulness/quality of the creative product, and not accuracy on a convergent creativity test. Scoring an output alone does not make it an in-scope with_ai outcome (codebook Sections 1 and 6; extraction rules 4-5). The numerical contrast is printed on PDF p. 12, Tables 5-6.

not_extracted.what: s1_analytical_growth_slope_chatgpt_vs_traditional: latent growth slope of analytical thinking
not_extracted.reason: Exclude the A-only estimate for the same construct boundary: growth in the separately scored analytical task is music-analysis competence, not creativity/diversity of the creative product or a convergent creativity test (PDF p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.6). The arm slopes are printed on PDF p. 9, Table 3, and described on PDF p. 8, Results RQ1; Table 3 supplies no between-arm slope test. Coding this separate competence outcome as other would not establish eligibility under extraction rule 4.

not_extracted.what: Initial creativity and analytical-thinking levels (latent intercepts)
not_extracted.reason: The intercepts describe starting performance, not effects on subsequent output. Baseline tasks are described as preceding intervention, although their exact mapping to Week 1 access is unclear. The analytical outcome is also outside the creativity scope. PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1 and Table 3.

not_extracted.what: Model-fit and assumption diagnostics, random intercept/slope variances, and intercept-slope covariances
not_extracted.reason: Model-fit indices, Box and Levene tests, residual diagnostics, individual variation, and baseline-growth associations are not AI-versus-control effects on an output outcome. Latent-factor variances are not observed-score SDs. PDF p. 6, Table 2; PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1-RQ2. No SDs were derived.

not_extracted.what: Effects of prior ChatGPT use and baseline creativity/analytical covariates
not_extracted.reason: Covariate effects do not estimate the randomized current instructional-group contrast. The instructional Group / Creativity row is extracted separately. PDF p. 9, Results RQ2; PDF pp. 11-12, Tables 4-5.

This omnibus test combines the eligible creativity score with the separate analytical competence outcome and does not isolate a creativity outcome. The creativity-specific univariate effect and adjusted means are retained. PDF p. 11, Table 4; PDF p. 9, Results RQ2.

not_extracted.what: Cross-lagged/autoregressive paths and endpoint creativity-analytical correlations
not_extracted.reason: These estimate associations between performances and compare those associations across groups, including adjustment for earlier post-assignment outcomes; they are not full-sample effects of AI on the creativity level of output. PDF pp. 9-10, Results RQ3; PDF p. 12, Table 7.

not_extracted.what: Epistemic network co-occurrences and weekly activation of creative idea, creative revision, analytical check, and analytical structure
not_extracted.reason: These are process analyses of the experimental group only, with no AI-versus-comparison-arm contrast. Move activation is not an output fluency or across-person diversity effect. PDF p. 10, Results RQ4; PDF pp. 13-14, Figures 3-4 and Table 8.

not_extracted.what: Markov transition probabilities between creative and analytical moves
not_extracted.reason: Transitions are derived from the experimental group only and describe interaction processes, with no randomized between-arm output contrast. PDF pp. 10-12, Results RQ5; PDF pp. 15-16, Figures 5-6.

not_extracted.what: Occasion-specific creativity means and endpoint values shown only as plotted growth trajectories
not_extracted.reason: Figure 1 supplies no numeric data labels for individual points. Reading values from the axes would require estimation, which is prohibited. The tabled latent growth slopes are retained instead. PDF p. 10, Figure 1; PDF p. 9, Table 3.

not_extracted.what: Separate originality, overall musical value, inventiveness, and expressive-impact rubric dimensions
not_extracted.reason: The four creativity dimensions are described but no dimension-specific arm levels or group contrasts are reported. The two reported analyses of the overall creativity score are retained as S1-O1 estimates. PDF p. 6, Section 3.3; PDF p. 9, Table 3; PDF p. 12, Tables 5-6.

open_items: The number of randomized classes per arm and the allocation procedure are unreported (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). The current codebook requires at least two classes per arm. The older screening-form claim that there is no minimum is superseded. The field_rct label records the explicit class-randomization claim; minimum-cluster eligibility cannot be confirmed, and these extracted results do not establish it.

Neither analysis reports uncertainty adjusted for randomized classes. The student-level SEs/tests must not be treated as independent-class precision; class identifiers and an analysis accounting for class assignment are needed before pooling. PDF pp. 8-9, Sections 3.7 and 4; PDF p. 12, Tables 5-6.

Participant-level observed creativity-score SDs by arm are not printed. Table 6 supplies adjusted-mean SEs and Table 3 supplies latent-parameter SEs; random-factor variances are different quantities. No SD or standardized mean difference was derived.
The MANCOVA dependent variable time point or aggregation is not specified (PDF p. 9, Results RQ2; PDF p. 12, Table 6).

The Week 1 covariates are called baseline scores and baseline tasks are described as pre-intervention, but Table 1 places AI-supported coursework in the opening weeks. Their exact timing relative to access is unclear. If they were measured after current treatment began, the adjusted estimate would fail extraction rule 5. PDF pp. 5-6 and 9.

Calendar weeks and measurement occasions are described inconsistently: weekly assessment, biweekly submissions across two semesters, and trajectories labeled across twelve weeks. The growth slope time unit cannot be confirmed. PDF pp. 5, 7-10.

The growth model does not print analysis-specific analyzed person counts, a between-arm slope test, difference SE, or interval. Within-arm p-value bounds are printed as < .000; they cannot be repaired from the source and are not between-arm p-values. PDF p. 9, Table 3.

Aggregation of rubric dimensions, external raters, and repeated products is unspecified, and inter-rater reliability for output scores is not reported. Interaction-log coding reliability is a separate measure. PDF pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5.
Earlier instructional-condition membership and its relation to current class allocation are unreported despite cohort overlap with Zhou and Kim (2024). PDF p. 5, Section 3.1.

The baseline-comparability statement cites Tables 1 and 2, which instead give instructional content and growth-model fit. The claimed balance test output is not provided, and the latent intercepts differ between groups. PDF pp. 5-6 and 9.

The screening form flags an internal inconsistency in Table 4's Group multivariate statistics. The PDF confirms the printed row, but the paper provides no correction. The joint creativity/analysis test is not extracted as a separate creativity outcome, and no statistic was recomputed. PDF p. 11, Table 4.

No appendix, supplement, or public dataset is identified in the saved article. Data are available on request from the corresponding author. Unreported counts, class identifiers, model definitions, and SDs remain unresolved. PDF p. 17, Data availability.
